# Longevity Weekly
> **Fourteen randomized trials showed resistance training raised handgrip strength in older adults with sarcopenia.**

**What You Need to Know:** Human randomized trials and meta-analyses demonstrate that resistance training improves muscle strength and physical performance measures such as gait speed in older adults with sarcopenia. These effects appear in both early and later stages of frailty. No regulator has approved any specific resistance training protocol for aging-related indications.

### The Week in Longevity
**Exercise slowed epigenetic aging in breast cancer survivors RCT:** A randomized controlled trial found that exercise slowed epigenetic aging among breast cancer survivors. The result comes from a human trial published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute. The trial measured epigenetic age markers before and after the exercise intervention in this specific population. Source: [academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/jnci/advance-article/doi/10.1093/jnci/djag296/8845541?searchresult=1)

**Retatrutide RCT for obesity published in NEJM:** The retatrutide randomized clinical trial for obesity, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, reported up to 30 percent loss of body weight versus placebo. Retatrutide is a triple receptor agonist acting on GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors. The trial confirmed marked potency of this triple receptor GLP-1 drug in participants with obesity. Source: [nejm.org](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2604169?query=featured_home)

**Exercise New Zealand spotlights research on muscle power’s association with longevity:** Exercise New Zealand highlighted observational research linking greater muscle power to longevity outcomes. The association rests on measures of physical function in older adults. The spotlight draws attention to how muscle power correlates with survival and independence measures. Source: [ausleisure.com.au](https://www.ausleisure.com.au/news/exercise-new-zealand-spotlights-research-on-muscle-powers-association-with-longevity)

**Regular Daily Routines Tied to Less Pain and Depression in Older Adults:** Observational data linked regular daily routines to lower levels of pain and depression in older adults. The finding comes from a cross-sectional analysis of routine stability. Participants with more consistent daily patterns showed reduced symptom scores on standardized assessments. Source: [thewellnews.com](https://www.thewellnews.com/health/regular-daily-routines-tied-to-less-pain-and-depression-in-older-adults/)

### Mechanism of the Week: Muscle, Strength and Aging
This week's mechanism examines how resistance training and related interventions influence sarcopenia and physical function in older adults. Sarcopenia describes the progressive loss of skeletal muscle mass, strength and physical function that occurs with advancing age and raises risks of frailty, falls and loss of independence. In one randomized controlled trial, sixty-eight community-dwelling older adults aged sixty-seven point two years on average with hamstring tightness and possible sarcopenia were randomly assigned to high-volume static stretching for thirty minutes daily, low-volume static stretching for three minutes three days per week, eccentric exercise or a non-intervention control for six weeks. Assessments conducted at baseline, post-intervention and three-month follow-up included muscle thickness, range of motion, musculotendinous unit stiffness, isometric knee flexor strength, cross-education effects on contralateral strength, Y-Balance performance and function outcomes. Significant group by time interaction effects were observed for range of motion and isometric strength. Eccentric exercise improved strength more than the control condition, whereas stretching-related changes remained below the minimal detectable change. No statistically detectable difference in range of motion was identified between high- and low-volume stretching. Low-volume stretching required substantially less weekly exercise time than high-volume stretching. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of fourteen randomized controlled trials in healthy older adults with sarcopenia found resistance training produced a standardized mean difference of zero point eight one for handgrip strength, one point two six for knee extension strength, one point two eight for gait speed and minus zero point nine three for the timed up and go test. A separate 2021 meta-analysis of twenty-five randomized trials with two thousand two hundred sixty-seven participants reported benefits on handgrip strength with an effect size of zero point five one, lower-limb strength with an effect size of zero point nine three, gait speed with an effect size of zero point seven five, functional performance with an effect size of zero point seven six and muscle mass with an effect size of zero point two nine. Resistance training during early stages had positive effects in all variables, being particularly effective in improving gait speed with an effect size of zero point six three and functional strength with an effect size of zero point five three. The PROVIDE study, a multicenter randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of three hundred eighty sarcopenic primarily independent-living older adults, showed that a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein nutritional supplement taken twice daily for thirteen weeks improved chair-stand time by one point zero one seconds and appendicular muscle mass by zero point one seven kilograms compared with an iso-caloric control. One meta-analysis found no statistically significant effect on appendicular skeletal muscle mass or skeletal muscle mass overall. No regulator has approved resistance training as a therapy for aging-related muscle loss. The effects on muscle mass were not consistent across studies. The mechanism acts on the hallmark of altered intercellular communication. The PROVIDE study was a completed randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial.

### Worth Knowing
- Randomized trials establish that resistance training improves strength and gait speed in older adults diagnosed with sarcopenia.
- Meta-analyses of human data show these strength gains occur in both early prevention and later treatment stages of frailty.
- Observational evidence connects higher muscle power to longevity, consistent with trial findings on physical performance.

### Evidence Ledger
- Resistance training produced a standardized mean difference of 0.81 for handgrip strength in a meta-analysis of fourteen randomized trials; evidence level is randomized human trial; source https://europepmc.org/article/MED/34763651.
- Resistance training improved handgrip strength with effect size 0.51 and lower-limb strength with effect size 0.93 across twenty-five randomized trials; evidence level is randomized human trial; source https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33921356.
- A vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein supplement improved chair-stand performance and appendicular muscle mass in a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 380 sarcopenic adults; evidence level is randomized human trial; source https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26170041.

### Trial Tracker
- PROVIDE study: vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein supplement versus iso-caloric control; randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial completed; no further dated milestone named in sources.

This is Longevity Weekly for September 30, 2026.

# Longevity Weekly
> **Phase 3 trials showed positive results for an autoimmune drug, an obesity maintenance regimen, and a gene therapy for a rare eye disease.**

**What You Need to Know:** This edition covers recent human trial results in autoimmune disease, obesity, and inherited eye conditions, plus observational data on cardiovascular health and insomnia treatment. It also introduces the hallmarks of aging framework used throughout the series to classify biological findings by evidence level. All reporting stays within published sources and states the type of evidence for each claim.

### What This Show Covers
The science of aging examines measurable biological processes that change over time and contribute to disease risk. The hallmarks framework organizes these processes into categories such as genomic instability, telomere attrition, epigenetic alterations, loss of proteostasis, disabled macroautophagy, deregulated nutrient-sensing, mitochondrial dysfunction, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion, altered intercellular communication, chronic inflammation, and dysbiosis. This episode uses the framework as its first worked example to separate cell or animal data from human outcomes and to note what remains untested in people. The show presents education only and never medical advice; every finding is labeled by evidence level so a mouse result is never presented as a human result. Longevity Weekly is part of the Nerra Network, an independent, ad-free network of shows at nerranetwork.com. Listeners can find the full archive and related programs at that site.

### The Week in Longevity
**Amgen reports a Phase 3 win with Sjögren’s drug candidate: BioPharma Dive**
Dazodalibep met its primary endpoint in one of two late-stage randomized human trials for Sjögren’s syndrome, an autoimmune disorder. The result comes from a Phase 3 study conducted after Amgen acquired the asset through its purchase of Horizon Therapeutics. The candidate targets the tough-to-treat condition via a mechanism acquired in the Horizon buyout. The trial represents the first of two planned late-stage studies. No regulatory decision on an aging-related indication has been reported. Source: [biopharmadive.com](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/amgen-dazodalibep-sjogrens-syndrome-study-results/831042/)

**Viking shares surge on updated obesity drug data: BioPharma Dive**
Participants in a randomized human trial maintained weight loss after switching from weekly to less frequent dosing of the company’s obesity drug. The maintenance data come from a late-stage study and were described by one analyst as strengthening competitive positioning. Trial participants largely sustained the weight reduction achieved on the initial weekly regimen. The findings address questions around dosing frequency in ongoing obesity treatment. No approval for aging-related use has been granted. Source: [biopharmadive.com](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/viking-obesity-drug-maintenance-study-results/831004/)

**Beacon eye gene therapy hits mark in late-stage study: BioPharma Dive**
A pivotal randomized trial of the gene therapy laru-zova met its primary endpoint in patients with X-linked retinitis pigmentosa. The result marks the first time a treatment for this inherited retinal condition achieved its main goal in a Phase 3 study. The trial evaluated the therapy in a population with the rare and potentially blinding disorder. Beacon presented the data as meeting the study’s primary objective. Regulatory review status has not been detailed in the report. Source: [biopharmadive.com](https://www.biopharmadive.com/news/beacon-xlrp-laru-zova-phase-3-study-results/830918/)

**Intermittent Fasting Shows Promise in a Huntington’s Trial: Lifespan.io**
A small pilot randomized human study found that intermittent fasting produced measurable improvements in patients with Huntington’s disease. The authors noted the limited sample size and called for larger trials before drawing firm conclusions. The pilot examined patients with this inherited neurodegenerative condition currently considered untreatable. Improvements were observed in disease-related measures during the fasting intervention. No regulatory body has approved intermittent fasting for this or any aging indication. Source: [lifespan.io](https://lifespan.io/intermittent-fasting-shows-promise-in-a-huntingtons-trial/)

**Treating insomnia with CBT-I may slow biological aging in older adults: Medical News Today**
An observational analysis linked cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia to slower epigenetic aging markers in older adults. The finding rests on biomarker associations rather than direct clinical outcomes and requires further randomized confirmation. The study examined older adults receiving CBT-I as treatment for insomnia. Epigenetic clocks served as the measure of biological aging change. Source: [medicalnewstoday.com](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/could-treating-insomnia-slow-biological-aging-study-finds-promising-link)

**Low Cardiovascular Risk in Early Midlife Correlates with Better Late Life Health: Fight Aging!**
Longitudinal observational data from several thousand participants showed that lower cardiovascular risk in the early forties correlated with reduced frailty and higher odds of reaching age 90. The spread in survival outcomes between lowest- and highest-risk groups reached six-fold in some metrics. The analysis processed data from a long-running study of midlife cardiovascular profiles. Researchers tracked frailty, quality of life, happiness, and well-being measures into old age. The analysis does not establish causation. Source: [fightaging.org](https://www.fightaging.org/archives/2026/09/low-cardiovascular-risk-in-early-midlife-correlates-with-better-late-life-health/)

### Mechanism of the Week: The Hallmarks of Aging
The hallmarks of aging are a set of twelve biological processes whose age-associated changes meet three criteria: they appear with advancing age, their experimental accentuation speeds aging, and their therapeutic targeting can slow, stop, or reverse aspects of aging in model systems. The original nine hallmarks were proposed in 2013 and later expanded to twelve to include disabled macroautophagy, chronic inflammation, and dysbiosis. Each hallmark describes a distinct but interconnected layer of cellular and tissue decline. Genomic instability refers to the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations; telomere attrition shortens chromosome ends and triggers DNA damage responses; epigenetic alterations change gene expression patterns without altering DNA sequence; loss of proteostasis impairs protein folding and clearance; disabled macroautophagy reduces the cell’s ability to recycle damaged components; deregulated nutrient-sensing disrupts pathways such as mTOR and AMPK that normally adjust metabolism to nutrient availability; mitochondrial dysfunction lowers energy production and increases reactive oxygen species; cellular senescence causes cells to stop dividing and secrete inflammatory signals; stem cell exhaustion depletes the pool of cells needed for tissue repair; altered intercellular communication changes signaling between cells; chronic inflammation sustains low-grade immune activation; and dysbiosis alters microbial communities that influence host metabolism and immunity. Evidence for the framework itself derives from reviews that compile cell, animal, and limited human observations rather than from any single randomized trial. The 2013 Cell paper enumerated the initial nine hallmarks and the 2023 update added three more while retaining the same three-premise test for inclusion. A 2020 review examined how metformin interacts with several hallmarks in cell and animal models, showing improvements in nutrient sensing, autophagy, and intercellular communication, yet noted that human outcome data remain limited to the ongoing TAME trial whose results are not yet available. Telomere studies illustrate how one hallmark can intersect with others, amplifying DNA damage responses and senescence, but these links rest primarily on cell and animal experiments. What is not established is whether intervening on any single hallmark produces consistent, clinically meaningful extension of healthy lifespan in humans; no hallmark-targeted therapy has received regulatory approval for an aging indication. Known risks of experimental interventions include off-target effects on cell proliferation or immune function, though specific safety profiles vary by agent and remain under study.

### Evidence Ledger
- The twelve hallmarks satisfy three premises of age association, experimental acceleration, and potential therapeutic reversal, as stated in a 2023 review. Evidence level: literature synthesis. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36599349)
- Metformin attenuates multiple hallmarks including nutrient sensing, autophagy, and intercellular communication in cell and animal models. Evidence level: cell and animal studies. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32333835)
- The original nine hallmarks were defined by the same three premises in a 2013 review. Evidence level: literature synthesis. Source: [europepmc.org](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/23746838)

### Trial Tracker
- TAME (Targeting Aging with Metformin): metformin, Phase 3 planning stage; next milestone not dated in sources.
- Viking obesity maintenance trial: unnamed obesity drug, late-stage; weight maintenance data reported.
- Beacon XLRP trial: laru-zova gene therapy, Phase 3; primary endpoint met.
- Huntington’s intermittent fasting pilot: intermittent fasting, pilot randomized; improvements observed, larger trials requested.

This episode marks the debut of Longevity Weekly.
